name: Hair gloss / glaze

card.summary: Shine glazes for salon-glossy hair; the effect is cosmetic and temporary, and no clinical studies of the products were found.
card.note: Sources did not describe gloss formulations specifically.

quick.overview:
Hair gloss or glaze treatments are used to make hair look shinier and smoother.

Reference material describes how conditioners and colorants affect shine, but no clinical studies of gloss products were found.
quick.mechanism: Treatments coat the hair or smooth the cuticle so light reflects more evenly. Laboratory work shows luster depends on hair structure and pigmentation [2].
quick.risks: Related color products may cause irritation or allergic reactions [1]; effects wash out over time.

lead: A hair gloss or glaze is a shine-boosting treatment used in salons and at home to make hair look glossier, smoother and richer in colour. People use it as a finishing step after colouring or bleaching, or on its own, because shiny hair reads as healthy and well kept, which lifts the overall polish of a person's look. The effect is temporary and gradually washes out. [1][4]

Encyclopedia coverage of hair colouring does not describe glosses or glazes by name, but it describes the product families they sit beside: toners that adjust undertones of bleached hair, and semi- and demi-permanent colourants that coat or sit beneath the cuticle and fade over several weeks of shampooing. [1] Conditioners are described as improving shine by coating the fibre, filling cuticle defects and flattening the cuticle scales, with silicones named for increasing shine. [4]

Shine relates to how light is scattered from the hair surface, and laboratory research has examined hair luster and how treatments change it. [2][3] No clinical studies of gloss or glaze products were found.

chain: Gloss or glaze is applied to cleansed hair
It coats the fibre and smooths cuticle scales (some products also add a sheer tint)
Hair reflects light more evenly and looks shinier and smoother until it washes out
angle.text: A gloss gives hair an immediate smoother, shinier finish, and tinted versions can freshen colour or tone down brassy undertones on bleached hair. Users apply it between or after colouring appointments to keep hair looking glossy. [1][4]

infobox: Conditioners, toners, semi- and demi-permanent colour [1][4]

paras: Gloss and glaze treatments are sold as salon services and home kits. Reference sources do not give a fixed formulation, and the products overlap with conditioners and low-lasting colour. A tinted gloss behaves like a semi-permanent colour, while a clear one acts more like a conditioning or shine-finishing treatment. [1][4]

Conditioners are described as improving shine by coating the fibre, filling cuticle defects and flattening cuticle scales. Washing with shampoo strips surface lipids, leaving hair rougher and more negatively charged, and conditioning counteracts this. Cationic surfactants such as cetrimonium chloride bind to hair and flatten the cuticle, acidifiers such as citric acid tighten it and reduce frizz, and silicones, most often dimethicone, form a thin film that fills cuticle defects, lowers friction and increases shine. [4]

Weathering, bleaching, dyeing and heat styling strip the cuticle's lipid film, leaving a rougher, more negatively charged surface. [4] Physical studies show that hair luster depends on the outer structure and pigmentation of the hair, not only on products applied. [2] Image analysis methods have been used to quantify how treatments change luster by measuring light reflected from curved hair tresses. [3]
Wikipedia describes toners as products that slightly alter the undertones of peroxide-bleached hair that has turned brassy or yellow, and purple shampoo as another way to counteract brassiness. [1]

Semi-permanent colorants contain no developer or ammonia and last about 4 to 8 shampoos; demi-permanent colours, which use an alkaline agent other than ammonia and little peroxide, give almost no lightening and fade over roughly 20 to 28 shampoos. Temporary colours sit on the surface and come out in one shampoo. [1]

Conditioners are available as rinse-out, deep conditioning masks, leave-in products and cleansing conditioners; leave-in types are formulated to be light and often contain silicones or polymers that also offer some thermal and UV protection. [4]

A 1991 optics paper investigated light scattering by individual human hairs and tied the intensity pattern to the arrangement of the outer structure and level of pigmentation, calculating contrast gloss values to quantify hair appearance. [2] A 2003 paper used image analysis of curved tresses to measure how treatments affect luster. [3]

A 2008 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Science followed long-term use of a scalp lotion containing eucalyptus extract, which increases ceramide in the skin, in Japanese women, older Japanese women, Japanese men and Caucasian women, and reported improved hair luster and bounce at the root. [5] A 2022 paper in ACS Omega compared silicone-free conditioner formulations with silicone-based ones on bleached Mongolian hair, reflecting industry interest in alternatives to silicones. [6] A 2024 paper established a UV-irradiated mouse model for hair luster, with oral minoxidil used to test reversibility. [7]

Safety concerns discussed for hair dyes include irritation and allergic reactions, with symptoms such as redness, itching and burning that may appear hours or a day later. [1] Water-insoluble silicones in conditioners can build up on hair, and cleansing conditioners are usually alternated with a clarifying shampoo; hard water deposits calcium and magnesium that can make hair rougher. [4] Wikipedia notes that claims of repair or fewer split ends are advertised benefits, not biological repair, because the hair shaft is made of dead cells. [4]
No studies found of gloss or glaze products. Related laboratory work covers hair luster measurement, conditioner and silicone-free formulations, and a scalp lotion tested on hair luster. [2][3][5][6]
